outputs.L1:
**After Po Chü-i, for Robert Creeley**

We don’t lack people here on the Northern coast,  
But they are people one meets, not people one cares for.  
So I bundle my daughters into the car  
And, with my brother poets, go to visit you, brother.

Here come your guests—a swarm of strangers and children;  
But the strangers write verses, and the children are daughters like yours.  
We bed down on mattresses and cots, roll up on the floor:  
Outside, burly old fruit trees stand in mist and rain;  
In every room, bundles sleep like larvae.

We waken and count our daughters. Otherwise, nothing happens.  
You feed them sweet rolls and melon, drive them all to the zoo;  
Patiently, patiently—ever the father—you answer their questions.  
Later, we eat again, drink, and listen to poems.

Nothing occurs, though we are aware you have three daughters  
Who, last year, were four.  
But even death becomes part of our ease:  
Poems, parenthood, sorrow—all we have learned  
From these of tenderness—hold us together  
At the center of life, entertaining daughters  
By firelight, with cake and songs.

You, my brother, are a good and violent drinker,  
Good at reciting short-line or long-line poems.  
In time, we will lose all our daughters, you and I,  
Be temperate, venerable, content to stay in one place,  
Sending our messages over the mountains and waters.
outputs.L2:
**In the spirit of Po Chü-i, for Robert Creeley**

The northern shore is hardly empty,  
yet those around us are acquaintances,  
not anyone we deeply love.  
I gather my daughters into the car  
and travel with fellow poets  
to see you, whom I call my brother.

Your visitors arrive in a crowd—  
unfamiliar adults mixed with children.  
Still, the adults are makers of poems,  
and the girls are daughters, just as yours are.

At night we spread ourselves everywhere:  
on camp beds and mattresses,  
or curled directly upon the floor.  
Beyond the house, thick-limbed, aging fruit trees  
stand beneath fog and rainfall.  
Inside, every room contains sleeping forms,  
wrapped and still as pupae.

Morning comes, and we make sure  
all our daughters are accounted for.  
Apart from that, there is no event.  
You give them melon and sugared buns,  
then take the whole company to the zoo.  
Again and again, with a father’s endurance,  
you respond to everything they ask.

Afterward there is more food,  
then drinking and the sound of poems.  
Once more, nothing remarkable takes place,  
although we remember that you now have three daughters  
where, a year ago, there were four.

Yet even loss settles into our shared comfort.  
Poetry, fatherhood, and grief—  
and the gentleness each has taught us—  
bind us at the heart of being alive,  
while we amuse our daughters beside the fire  
with singing and slices of cake.

Brother, you drink fiercely and well,  
and you speak poems skillfully,  
whether their lines are brief or extended.

Someday both of us will have let  
all our daughters go.  
We will become restrained, honored old men,  
satisfied to remain where we are,  
sending words to one another  
across rivers, seas, and mountain ranges.
outputs.L3:
The speaker travels with his daughters and a group of fellow poets to visit Robert Creeley, a man he regards not merely as a friend but as a brother. Their time together is modest and crowded, shaped by the ordinary routines of shared family life: finding places for everyone to sleep, eating meals, taking the children to the zoo, drinking, talking, and reading or writing poetry. These simple activities create an atmosphere of warmth and closeness in which domestic life and artistic fellowship become inseparable.

Creeley emerges as a patient, tender father. He looks after the children carefully, listens to them, and answers their questions with kindness. At the same time, the death of one of his daughters remains a quiet presence throughout the visit. The grief is never erased, but neither does it overwhelm the gathering. Instead, it is absorbed into the families’ intimacy, becoming part of their shared experience of love, loss, and continuing life.

Looking toward the future, the speaker imagines himself and Creeley growing old. Their daughters will eventually become adults and leave them, creating new distances and forms of absence. Yet the bond between the two poets will endure. Even when separated by great distances, they will continue to exchange poems, sustaining their brotherhood through language, memory, and the lasting intimacy of their art.
outputs.L4:
The poem recounts a family visit to the poet Robert Creeley, transforming a sequence of ordinary domestic moments into a meditation on friendship, art, and mortality. Travel, shared meals, childcare, conversation, and drinking create an atmosphere of intimacy in which poetry is inseparable from daily life. The poets are not presented as distant literary figures but as parents and friends whose creative work emerges alongside practical responsibilities, affection, fatigue, and companionship.

Throughout the visit, small gestures carry emotional weight. Caring for children, eating together, and exchanging poems become ways of sustaining one another. Art does not offer an escape from ordinary experience; instead, it deepens the participants’ awareness of it. Parenthood likewise makes them more vulnerable to fear and loss, even as it gives them a powerful reason to remain attentive to the present.

Sorrow and the knowledge of death shadow these scenes. The friends understand that their time together is temporary and that future separation is unavoidable. Yet this awareness does not overwhelm the poem. Rather, it intensifies the tenderness among them, allowing friendship to become a defense against isolation and despair.

In the end, the poem suggests that poetry, family life, and shared grief form a bond strong enough to resist—though not defeat—mortality. By gathering around food, children, drink, conversation, and art, the friends create a temporary refuge at the heart of existence. Their closeness sustains them against death and future loss, keeping them, for a time, at the living center of the world.

### Robert Creeley and the Northern Landscape

Robert Creeley was an influential American poet whose spare, fragmented style reshaped modern poetry. Born in Massachusetts and later associated with Black Mountain College, Creeley often used short lines, pauses, and ordinary language to capture the rhythms of thought and speech.

A northern atmosphere runs quietly through much of his life and work. New England’s restraint, its changing seasons, and its austere landscapes seem reflected in the economy of his poems. Creeley rarely offered elaborate descriptions; instead, he reduced experience to essential words, leaving silence and empty space to carry emotional weight.

His long connection with Buffalo, New York, where he taught for many years, strengthened this northern identity. The cold, industrial city provided an appropriate setting for poetry concerned with solitude, memory, love, and human vulnerability. In Creeley’s writing, the North is not simply a geographical region. It becomes a state of mind—clear, difficult, intimate, and stripped to its foundations.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem titled “after Po Chü-i, for Robert Creeley” about poets visiting one another with their daughters, sharing food, poetry, grief, and friendship.
counterfactuals.output:
# after Po Chü-i, for Robert Creeley

You came by the river road  
with your daughter.  
Mine ran out barefoot  
to meet her.

We set rice on the table,  
greens, a little fish,  
the wine saved  
for no occasion.

The girls divided a peach  
and laughed at the stone.  
We read each other  
three short poems.

Between the second  
and the third,  
you spoke the name  
of one who had died.

Evening entered the room.  
No one moved  
to light the lamp.

At last the children  
fell asleep together,  
their hands open  
on the same quilt.

Old friend,  
how little we had—  
food, words, sorrow—

and how completely  
we gave it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a free-verse epistolary poem in the style of Po Chü-i, addressed to Robert Creeley, blending domestic tenderness, parenthood, loss, drinking, and literary brotherhood.
counterfactuals.output:
**Letter to Robert Creeley, After the Children Sleep**

Dear Robert—

Tonight the kettle mutters  
on the blue flame.

My daughter has left one shoe  
beneath the table,  
my son a wooden horse  
fallen on its side.

I do not set them right.

All day we teach the house  
to bear our weight:  
bread cut unevenly,  
small socks at the stove,  
a cup chipped at the lip  
but still in use.

You knew how few words  
a life will stand.

Outside, rain gathers  
in the empty flowerpots.  
Inside, my wife turns in sleep  
and reaches across the bed  
for the warmth I have carried  
to this desk.

Robert, I pour two cups.

One for the living,  
one for those who have gone  
where letters arrive  
without an answer.

The wine is cheap.  
It catches the lamp  
and becomes, briefly,  
a better autumn.

I drink to my father,  
whose hands I remember  
more clearly than his voice;

to the child we did not keep,  
that small room in the heart  
we enter without knocking;

to friends whose books remain  
upright on the shelf  
while their bodies  
have lain down.

What is poetry now?

A coat over a sleeping child.  
A bowl washed late.  
The name of a brother  
spoken into weather.

You made the line narrow  
so sorrow could cross it  
without falling.

I have tried, too,  
to say only what the table knows:  
wood wears smooth under elbows,  
hunger returns,  
the beloved grows older  
while we look away.

Near midnight  
the house gives one soft crack.

Perhaps the cold.  
Perhaps the dead  
shifting their chairs  
to hear us better.

I lift my cup.

Brother, wherever you are,  
may there be plain bread,  
good silence,  
and someone coming home  
through the snow.

Here, morning is not far off.

Soon the children will wake  
and ask for water,  
for stories,  
for the whole world  
again.

I will give what I can.

The rest, Robert,  
I send to you.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a narrative poem about bundling several daughters into a car to visit a fellow poet on the Northern coast, where everyone sleeps on floors, visits the zoo, eats cake, and recites poems.
counterfactuals.output:
### Northbound with Daughters

We packed the girls like quilts into the car—  
knees, ribbons, paper dolls, a red tin pail—  
and pointed north, where gulls stitched up the sky  
above the dark, salt-breathing coast.

All morning the road unrolled its gray instruction.  
The daughters sang, then quarreled, slept, awoke,  
asked if the sea was near, if poems could swim,  
if poets always lived where the wind was loud.

At last, our friend stood waving by her gate,  
her hair blown sideways, laughing at our cargo.  
Her house was small; the rooms filled up at once  
with shoes and coats and seven kinds of chatter.

That night we spread ourselves across the floors—  
blankets between bookcases, pillows under chairs.  
The children dreamed in heaps, like fallen blossoms;  
the poets whispered late beside the stove.

Next day, the zoo: a bear paced out a stanza,  
the seals applauded every silver dive,  
a solemn owl revised the afternoon,  
and monkeys stole the daughters’ careful manners.

We came home wind-flushed, ravenous, and bright.  
Someone lit candles on a lopsided cake.  
Crumbs jeweled the boards; the youngest licked the icing;  
the eldest wished her wish and would not tell.

Then poems began—first shyly, then like weather.  
One voice raised the roof; one hushed the room.  
The girls sat still, astonished that their mothers  
could summon wolves and moons from printed marks.

Outside, the northern ocean struck its drum.  
Inside, we passed the pages hand to hand,  
while children folded into sleep around us  
and every floorboard seemed to learn a song.

At dawn we bundled daughters back in coats,  
counted them twice, and turned the car toward home.  
Behind us, our friend grew small beside the sea,  
still waving as the poems followed northwind—

or followed us: in cake tins, tangled blankets,  
in zoo cries, salt hair, elbows, dreams, and shoes—  
the whole car humming, crowded past its windows  
with all the lives a single journey holds.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an intimate contemporary poem in which two brother poets and their families spend an uneventful but meaningful visit together, reflecting on a deceased child and the eventual loss of all their daughters.
counterfactuals.output:
**What We Did That Sunday**

My brother brought his wife and girls  
in a car powdered with road salt.  
We stood in the driveway too long,  
touching shoulders, taking bags  
no one needed help with.

Inside, the kettle clicked off.  
Our daughters moved from room to room,  
borrowing sweaters, comparing scars,  
their laughter arriving through the walls  
like sun through winter branches.

Nothing happened. We ate soup.  
The men washed dishes; the women  
corrected our way of drying them.  
A dog slept beneath the table,  
dreaming with one black paw raised.

Once, my brother said the name  
of the child who had died—  
not ceremonially, only because  
the blue cup had been his,  
and someone asked.

For a moment the house held still,  
though the girls went on upstairs,  
dragging chairs, singing half a song.  
Grief had learned to live among us  
without needing its own room.

Near dusk we walked to the field.  
The daughters ran ahead,  
their coats open despite the cold,  
each one already practicing  
the beautiful work of leaving.

My brother and I lagged behind.  
We spoke of poems, which meant  
we spoke of time: how it takes  
every child, one way or another—  
into silence, marriage, distance,

into lives whose doors close softly  
after us. We knew we would lose  
all our daughters. We knew  
this was not tragedy, not always.  
Still, knowledge darkened the snow.

At the cars we embraced again.  
Someone forgot a glove. Someone  
came back for it. Then taillights  
diminished along the road  
until the road was empty.

Nothing had happened all day.  
Yet cups stood cooling in the sink,  
beds held the shapes of coats,  
and every room seemed larger  
for having briefly been full.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a restrained, conversational homage to Robert Creeley that contrasts loneliness with the warmth of poets, children, firelight, food, songs, and messages sent across mountains and waters.
counterfactuals.output:
I can’t write in Robert Creeley’s exact style, but I can offer a spare, conversational poem with short lines, pauses, and intimate, plainspoken warmth.

**News from Far Away**

Loneliness comes  
without knocking,  
sits in the chair  
by the cold window.

Then someone reads  
a poem aloud.

A child laughs  
in the next room.  
The fire finds  
another log.

Bread is cut,  
soup passed hand  
to hand. Someone  
starts an old song,

not well,  
but enough.

And from beyond  
the mountains,  
across dark water,

a message arrives:

I am here.  
Are you there?

For a while  
the whole house  
answers.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
